terms.grammar: adverbs, with the stressed word between them
evidence: Ps.-Publ. A 23: Amīcum laedere nē jocō quidem licet.
Cic. Fin. 5.55: conquiēscere nē īnfantēs quidem possint
terms.comment: The word that is stressed stands between nē and quidem: nē jocō quidem, not even as a joke. It also gives “not … either”: nē ego quidem, nor do I. After nōn modo, “not only not … but not even”: nōn modo … sed nē … quidem.

phrases.latin: Amīcum laedere nē jocō quidem licet.
phrases.english: You may not hurt a friend, not even as a joke.

phrases.latin: vidēmus igitur ut conquiēscere nē īnfantēs quidem possint
phrases.english: so we see that not even babies can keep still

phrases.latin: nē exspectēmus quidem, dum rogēmur; studium semper adsit, cūnctātiō absit
phrases.english: let us not even wait to be asked; let eagerness always be there, and hesitation never

phrases.latin: nōn assuēscat ergō, nē dum īnfāns quidem est, sermōnī quī dēdiscendus sit
phrases.english: so let him not get used, not even while he is a baby, to speech he will have to unlearn

sources: Lewis & Short: ne · Lewis & Short: quidem
